interactions.label: A young woman has a clear-to-white vaginal discharge that increases at mid-cycle

params.question: A young woman has a clear-to-white vaginal discharge that increases at mid-cycle and premenstrually. It is odourless and non-itchy, and her vaginal pH is 4.2. Which feature MOST reliably distinguishes this as physiological leucorrhoea rather than an infective discharge?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sexual activity status does not define the nature of vaginal discharge; infections such as candidiasis can occur without sexual contact. The key discriminator is the cyclical hormonal pattern.

answers.text: The discharge volume varies with the menstrual cycle phase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cyclical variation driven by oestrogen — increasing at ovulation and premenstrually — is the hallmark of physiological leucorrhoea, distinguishing it from infective causes.

answers.text: The discharge has persisted for several months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Duration alone does not differentiate; both physiological discharge and chronic infections can persist for months. Look for the cyclical pattern and absence of odour, itch, and raised pH.

answers.text: The discharge is visible at the external cervical os

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both physiological secretions and pathological discharges can be visible at the cervical os; this finding alone is not discriminatory.

overallFeedback.feedback: The hallmark of physiological leucorrhoea is its cyclical variation with oestrogen — peaking at ovulation and premenstrually — combined with normal pH, no odour, and no itch.

Correct! Physiological leucorrhoea varies with oestrogen levels — peaking at ovulation and premenstrually. This cyclical pattern, along with normal pH and absence of odour or itch, distinguishes it from infection.

interactions.label: A postmenopausal woman and a young woman on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics

params.question: A postmenopausal woman and a young woman on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics both present with symptomatic vaginal discharge. What is the shared underlying mechanism that predisposes them to infection?

answers.text: Both conditions cause direct invasion by pathogenic bacteria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neither oestrogen deficiency nor antibiotics directly introduce pathogens. Both disrupt the lactobacillus-mediated defence, and the resulting pH rise is what permits secondary colonisation.

answers.text: Both conditions cause atrophy of the vaginal epithelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Epithelial atrophy occurs in oestrogen-deficient states like menopause but not with antibiotics. The shared mechanism is disruption of the lactobacillus-dependent acidic environment.

answers.text: Both result in loss of the lactobacillus-maintained acidic vaginal environment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In menopause, oestrogen loss depletes glycogen and starves lactobacilli; antibiotics kill lactobacilli directly. Both routes break the same oestrogen–glycogen–lactobacillus–lactic acid axis, raising pH.

answers.text: Both conditions introduce alkaline substances into the vaginal environment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neither condition introduces alkaline substances. The pH rises because lactobacillus numbers fall — through glycogen depletion or direct killing — reducing lactic acid production.

overallFeedback.feedback: The shared mechanism is disruption of the lactobacillus-maintained acidic environment. Menopause depletes glycogen via oestrogen loss; antibiotics kill lactobacilli directly — both break the same protective axis.
Correct! Both menopause (glycogen depletion) and antibiotics (direct lactobacillus killing) disrupt the same protective axis, causing pH to rise and leaving the vagina vulnerable to infection.

params.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a thin, grey-white vaginal discharge that has a fishy odour, especially noticeable after intercourse. She denies itching or vulval soreness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thin, grey-white discharge with a fishy (amine) odour and notably no itching is the classic presentation. The absence of itch distinguishes BV from candidiasis.
Candidiasis presents with intense itching, thick curdy discharge, and vulval erythema — none present here. The absence of itch strongly argues against it.
Trichomoniasis produces a profuse, frothy, yellow-green discharge with soreness and often a strawberry cervix. This patient's thin, grey-white, non-irritating discharge does not fit.
Physiological leucorrhoea is odourless. A fishy odour is pathological and points to amine production in bacterial vaginosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct diagnosis is bacterial vaginosis: thin, grey-white discharge with a fishy odour and no itching. Remember: no itch + amine smell = BV; intense itch + curdy discharge = candidiasis; frothy yellow-green = trichomoniasis.
Correct! The 'no itch + fishy odour' combination is the clinical signature of bacterial vaginosis, distinguishing it from the intense itch of candidiasis and the frothy discharge of trichomoniasis.

interactions.label: A 24-year-old woman is diagnosed with trichomoniasis. Her male partner is asympt

params.question: A 24-year-old woman is diagnosed with trichomoniasis. Her male partner is asymptomatic and reluctant to take medication. What is the correct advice regarding his treatment?

answers.text: Partner treatment is optional since he has no symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Asymptomatic carriage is common in male partners with trichomoniasis. Without concurrent treatment, the woman will be reinfected after completing her own course.

answers.text: Partner treatment can be deferred until his test results are available

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting for test results delays treatment and permits reinfection. Both partners must be treated simultaneously in trichomoniasis, regardless of the partner's test status.

answers.text: Only the woman needs treatment if she avoids intercourse until her course is complete

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Even with abstinence during treatment, the partner remains a reservoir. Reinfection will occur when intercourse resumes unless he is also treated.

answers.text: Partner treatment is mandatory; without it, reinfection is almost certain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Trichomoniasis is a true sexually transmitted infection, so untreated partners harbour the parasite even without symptoms. This differs from BV and candidiasis, which do not routinely require partner treatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: Partner treatment is mandatory for trichomoniasis because it is a true STI — without concurrent treatment, reinfection is almost certain. BV and candidiasis do not routinely require partner treatment.
Correct! Trichomoniasis is a true STI, so partner treatment is always mandatory. This differs from BV and candidiasis, where routine partner treatment is unnecessary.
